justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across the three time horizons, starting near 95.1 for the one-day horizon and edging toward 96.5 by the one-month mark. The one-day estimate was anchored primarily by recent price momentum and short-term mean-reversion tendencies — markets rarely make large moves in a single session absent a major catalyst, so the estimate stays close to the last observed level. The slight upward bias over the week and month reflects a general assumption of a modestly positive drift consistent with historical equity risk premiums, combined with an absence of any strongly bearish macro signals at the time of the forecast. In essence, the base case assumed continuation of prevailing conditions rather than a regime change.

The confidence interval widths widen considerably as the horizon extends, which reflects the compounding of uncertainty over time. For the one-day window, the interval is relatively tight at roughly plus or minus 2.6 points, consistent with typical daily realized volatility for the instrument in question. By the one-week horizon, that spread roughly doubles, and by one month it expands to nearly 19 points on the full interval width. This scaling is broadly consistent with a square-root-of-time volatility model, though I also layered in some additional uncertainty at longer horizons to account for the possibility of macroeconomic or policy surprises that are harder to anticipate over weeks than over hours.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected deterioration in macroeconomic data — such as a surprise in inflation figures, employment reports, or central bank communications signaling a more hawkish pivot — could produce a rapid repricing that breaks below the lower bound, particularly at the one-month horizon. A geopolitical escalation or financial contagion event would similarly compress risk appetite well beyond what daily volatility assumptions would suggest. On the upside, a surprisingly strong earnings season, a dovish policy surprise, or a resolution of existing geopolitical tensions could propel the instrument above the upper bound of the one-month interval. The tails at the monthly horizon are genuinely fat, and the 90% interval, while wide, does not fully capture the most extreme scenarios.

It is worth acknowledging that these forecasts carry inherent limitations. The point estimates assume a relatively smooth continuation of recent dynamics and do not account for structural breaks or liquidity crises. The confidence intervals are derived from historical volatility patterns, which can understate risk during periods of market stress when correlations spike and liquidity thins. In short, the intervals should be read as a probabilistic guide rather than a hard boundary, and real-world outcomes at the one-month horizon especially should be expected to occasionally fall well outside what is stated here.
